title: Tips for adults living with hearing loss or deafness
intro: Hearing loss can make conversation, work and social life more tiring, but practical strategies help. Small changes in the way you and others communicate, together with technology and support services, make daily life easier. Asking for what you need is a skill worth practising.

sections.heading: Making conversations easier
paragraphs: Face the person you are talking to and ensure good light on their face so you can see lip movements and expressions. Choose quiet places, reduce background noise, and ask others to speak clearly at a normal pace without shouting or exaggerating. Ask them to rephrase instead of repeating the same words. Be open about your hearing loss, so people understand.

sections.heading: Using technology
paragraphs: Hearing aids and cochlear implants help many people, and should be worn consistently and fitted by an audiologist. Add-ons such as remote microphones, television streamers and loop systems improve understanding in difficult settings. Captions and subtitles on video, speech-to-text apps and amplified telephones help with media and calls. Flashing or vibrating alarms and doorbells make home safer.

sections.heading: At work and in public
paragraphs: Tell your employer what helps, such as meeting in quiet rooms, written agendas, captioned video meetings or sign-language interpreters. Many countries give legal rights to reasonable adjustments. In public places, ask about hearing loops and written information, and choose seats close to the speaker.

sections.heading: Looking after yourself
paragraphs: Listening is tiring, so schedule breaks and quiet time. Protect remaining hearing from loud noise. Have hearing tested regularly, and treat ear problems promptly. Stay socially connected, as isolation raises the risk of loneliness and low mood. Peer groups and hearing loss organisations offer advice and shared experience.

sections.heading: Involving family and friends
paragraphs: Explain to family and friends how to communicate with you, for example by getting your attention before speaking and not talking from another room. Agree on signals when you do not understand. Learning lip-reading or sign language, alone or together with family, can enrich communication.

examples.title: Preparing for a meeting
examples.text: Imagine you have a team meeting. You could ask for the agenda in advance, sit facing the speaker and request that people speak one at a time.

examples.title: Setting up at home
examples.text: Suppose you struggle to hear the television. You might ask an audiologist about a streamer or headphones that connect to the TV.
